p.src: Real choice is rarely a choice between pure good and pure evil. If one option is entirely good and another is entirely bad, there is no serious choice. A normal mind can decide. That opportunity is slow but durable. This person is talented but unreliable. That market is small but expanding. This habit is comfortable but decays attention. That habit is difficult but compounds.

p.src: This chain is not mystical. It is ordinary causality. Concepts shape what you can see. Values shape what you rank. Ranking shapes what you choose. Choice shapes action. Repeated action shapes fate.

p.src: A useful decision practice is to pause before important choices and write the ranking explicitly:

u.src: A useful decision practice is to pause before important choices and write the ranking explicitly:
en: A useful decision practice is to pause before important choices and write the ranking explicitly:

p.src: What options am I considering, including doing nothing?

u.src: What options am I considering, including doing nothing?
en: What options am I considering, including doing nothing?

p.src: What is good about each option?

u.src: What is good about each option?
en: What is good about each option?

p.src: What is bad about each option?

u.src: What is bad about each option?
en: What is bad about each option?

p.src: Which benefits are short-term, and which benefits compound?

u.src: Which benefits are short-term, and which benefits compound?
en: Which benefits are short-term, and which benefits compound?

p.src: Which costs are visible now, and which costs will appear later?

u.src: Which costs are visible now, and which costs will appear later?
en: Which costs are visible now, and which costs will appear later?

p.src: What value is controlling my current preference?

u.src: What value is controlling my current preference?
en: What value is controlling my current preference?

p.src: Am I overgeneralizing from my own experience or my own circle?

u.src: Am I overgeneralizing from my own experience or my own circle?
en: Am I overgeneralizing from my own experience or my own circle?

p.src: What evidence from outside my circle should I gather before deciding?

u.src: What evidence from outside my circle should I gather before deciding?
en: What evidence from outside my circle should I gather before deciding?

p.src: The act of writing matters. Thinking silently allows vague preference to disguise itself as judgment. Writing forces the mind to expose its ranking rules.

p.src: Reviewing Past Choices

u.src: Reviewing Past Choices
en: Reviewing Past Choices

p.src: The best place to begin is not a future fantasy. It is a past decision.

u.src: The best place to begin is not a future fantasy. It is a past decision.
en: The best place to begin is not a future fantasy. It is a past decision.

p.src: Choose three to five important choices from your own life. A job accepted. A job refused. A business started. A skill ignored. A relationship entered. An investment made. An opportunity missed. A habit tolerated. A city chosen. A debt taken. A year wasted.

u.src: Choose three to five important choices from your own life. A job accepted. A job refused. A business started. A skill ignored. A relationship entered. An investment made. An opportunity missed. A habit tolerated. A city chosen. A debt taken. A year wasted.

p.src: For each choice, review it as calmly as possible:

u.src: For each choice, review it as calmly as possible:
en: For each choice, review it as calmly as possible:

p.src: What did I choose?

u.src: What did I choose?
en: What did I choose?

p.src: What did I believe at the time?

u.src: What did I believe at the time?
en: What did I believe at the time?

p.src: What did I value more than other things?

u.src: What did I value more than other things?
en: What did I value more than other things?

p.src: Which value was useful?

u.src: Which value was useful?
en: Which value was useful?

p.src: Which value was confused?

u.src: Which value was confused?
en: Which value was confused?

p.src: Where did I mistake a partial view for the whole?

u.src: Where did I mistake a partial view for the whole?
en: Where did I mistake a partial view for the whole?

p.src: What principle would have helped me choose better?

u.src: What principle would have helped me choose better?
en: What principle would have helped me choose better?

p.src: This exercise is not for self-punishment. Punishment does not improve values. Clear review does. The point is to find the ranking rule that produced the choice. If the ranking rule was wrong, the future must not be left to the same rule.

u.src: This exercise is not for self-punishment. Punishment does not improve values. Clear review does. The point is to find the ranking rule that produced the choice. If the ranking rule was wrong, the future must not be left to the same rule.

p.src: For example, a person may discover that he repeatedly valued immediate safety above long-term growth. Another may discover that he valued approval above truth. Another may have valued busyness above leverage. Another may have valued being right above becoming stronger. Another may have valued comfort above attention. Each discovery is a chance to rewrite the operating system.

p.src: Do Not Worship Intuition

u.src: Do Not Worship Intuition
en: Do Not Worship Intuition

p.src: Some people defend their choices by saying, It was my intuition.

u.src: Some people defend their choices by saying, It was my intuition.
en: Some people defend their choices by saying, It was my intuition.

p.src: Intuition can be useful, but only when it is the compressed result of long, relevant experience. A veteran may see a pattern quickly because he has seen thousands of cases. A beginner’s intuition is often only fear, desire, memory, or ego wearing a confident mask.

u.src: Intuition can be useful, but only when it is the compressed result of long, relevant experience. A veteran may see a pattern quickly because he has seen thousands of cases. A beginner’s intuition is often only fear, desire, memory, or ego wearing a confident mask.

p.src: The question is not whether intuition feels strong. Feelings often feel strong. The question is whether the intuition was trained by repeated contact with reality and corrected by feedback.

u.src: The question is not whether intuition feels strong. Feelings often feel strong. The question is whether the intuition was trained by repeated contact with reality and corrected by feedback.
en: The question is not whether intuition feels strong. Feelings often feel strong. The question is whether the intuition was trained by repeated contact with reality and corrected by feedback.

p.src: When intuition appears, inspect it:

u.src: When intuition appears, inspect it:
en: When intuition appears, inspect it:

p.src: What experience trained this intuition?

u.src: What experience trained this intuition?
en: What experience trained this intuition?

p.src: How many comparable cases have I actually seen?

u.src: How many comparable cases have I actually seen?
en: How many comparable cases have I actually seen?

p.src: When has this intuition been wrong before?

u.src: When has this intuition been wrong before?
en: When has this intuition been wrong before?

p.src: What data would I seek if I did not trust the feeling?

u.src: What data would I seek if I did not trust the feeling?
en: What data would I seek if I did not trust the feeling?

p.src: This does not kill intuition. It disciplines it. A disciplined intuition can become a valuable tool. An undisciplined intuition is only another path into overgeneralization.

u.src: Different Values, Different Lives

p.src: People do not need to share identical values. The purpose of refining values is not to prove that everyone else is wrong. The purpose is to make one’s own life better.

p.src: This matters because values are easy to turn into performance. A person discovers a clearer ranking and immediately wants to lecture others. But other people’s values are not the main problem. Your own choices are.

p.src: If your values become slightly clearer, your next choices become slightly better. If your choices become slightly better, your actions become slightly better. If this repeats long enough, the difference becomes visible in your life. That is enough reason to begin.

p.src: Values also change through practice. A person may say he values attention, but if he spends every spare hour in distraction, his real value is comfort. A person may say he values freedom, but if he never accumulates skill, capital, or leverage, his real value is familiarity. A person may say he values truth, but if he cannot tolerate correction, his real value is face.

p.src: Fate is often invoked after the result is already bad. People look backward and say, It was fate, as if the outcome descended from the sky. But many outcomes were built earlier, at the moment of choice, and the choice was built earlier still, in the values that ranked the options.

p.src: This does not mean we control everything. We do not. Luck, history, health, family, markets, policy, timing, and other people all matter. But the part we can influence is large enough to deserve seriousness.

p.src: A person who improves his values improves the source of his choices. He becomes less likely to spend years solving the wrong problem. He becomes less likely to mistake approval for truth, busyness for progress, safety for life, or personal need for market demand. He becomes more able to step outside himself, gather evidence, accept feedback, and choose again.
